property_summary: For any nonzero newOwner address, transferOwnership can be called by the current owner and results in owner() == newOwner (reference enforces newOwner != address(0) so calling with address(0) reverts; the mutant allows setting owner to zero so behavior for newOwner==address(0) differs), and thus there exists an input (newOwner == address(0)) where the mutant accepts the call while the reference reverts.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) always reverts when newOwner == address(0) on the reference (it forbids zero address), whereas the mutant allows setting owner to address(0) (i.e. does not revert for newOwner == address(0)); thus the property: if msg.sender == owner then transferOwnership(address(0)) must revert (reference satisfies for all inputs), which the mutant violates for some input.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership with any newOwner that is non-equal to the caller must either (a) set owner() to newOwner if newOwner != address(0) or (b) revert if newOwner == address(0); in particular the reference contract always reverts when the current owner calls transferOwnership(address(0)) while the mutant sometimes succeeds — so the property: when the current owner calls transferOwnership(newOwner) the call must revert if and only if newOwner == address(0).

For any caller who is NOT the current owner, transferOwnership(newOwner) must always revert (only the owner can transfer); the mutant can break this by allowing a non-owner to transfer ownership to address(0) if some caller dynamics differ, so the reference always reverts for non-owners while the mutant may not.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) either succeeds and sets owner() == newOwner when newOwner != address(0), or else reverts when newOwner == address(0); the mutant (which removes the non-zero check) will allow a call with newOwner == address(0) to succeed and set owner() to zero — violating the rule.

For any caller X, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) succeeds (does not revert) on the reference contract exactly when msg.sender == owner(), but the mutant that additionally requires tx.origin == owner() will wrongly reject legitimate calls where a contract (with msg.sender == owner via a delegate/forward) mediates the call — i.e. the reference allows the owner to call through a contract proxy (msg.sender == owner) while the mutant rejects when tx.origin differs.
